elements.text:
This is how complex systems are designed
today. 

It allows the system to grow as you can
keep adding servers. 

The load balancer takes a big relevance here
as it will be in charge of distribute the
requests among the available servers. 

LB can work with different algorithms some
of them are: 
- Randomly picking the server. 
- Based on the server capacity and try to
route traffic inteligently.

If a server is down, the load balancer will
noticed that and route the traffic to the
others servers.

Web servers needs to be stateless.

- We cannot assume that our server will
know anything about previous requests. 

- Each call the LB will route traffic to
probably different servers.

- We can of course save information in the
database.

elements.text:
Periodic Backup
- Backup of the database will be saved periodically
to a replacement database. 

- We will have to have some tolerance with some data
being lost and a decent amount of time with the
system down. Maybe for admin tools, or internal
tools.

- Is cheap 

Downsides:
- Increase the amount of downside, we need to
provision the new server and load the data into the
new DB. Depending on the amount of data, that can
take hours - days.

- Any data that happens after the BU creation will
be lost.

elements.text:
- Most databases will have the replication feature so
we turn it on and the database will start saving to
the replicate database.  

- We can also manually save the information to the
replicated database. 

- Replicated DB will be always "warm" so it will have
the data ready to be used. 

- The down window is really short, we just have to
redirect the traffic to the replicated database if the
primary DB is down. 

- Very little or non data is lost. 

Downsides.

elements.text:
- The standby database will be replicated in
real time. 

- We can use that standby database as
another read source. 

- If the connection is lost with the primary DB
then we can switch and start reading directly
from the replicated database. 

Difference with Warm
- We are doing the replication in real time so
there is no delay.

- We are writing simultaneusly to both
databases from our web server. 

- We are not relying anymore in
replication. We will have two primary
databases ready to go live always. 

- The problem that needs to be solved
is the synchronisation between them if
one of them go down and we rely on the
other, meaning that until recovery we
will only be writing to one PDB.

elements.text:
We split a large dataset into smaller partitions called shards. Each shard contains a subset of the data and can live on a different server. The system uses a sharding key,
like userId or tenantId, to decide where each record belongs. This helps scale storage and write throughput horizontally, but it introduces complexity with cross-shard
queries, joins, rebalancing, and distributed transactions.

- Sharding = scalability
- Replication = availability/resilience

We split a large dataset into smaller partitions called shards. Each shard contains a subset of the data and can live on a different server. The system uses a sharding key, like userId or tenantId, to decide where each record belongs. This helps scale storage and write throughput horizontally, but it introduces complexity with cross-shard queries, joins, rebalancing, and distributed transactions.

- Sharding = scalability
- Replication = availability/resilience

elements.text:
How is data divided between shards? 

- Normally, we will set up some rules for data to be saved
on each shard (partition) by an specific rule. 
    E.g.
    - Shard 1 -> UserId > 0 && userId <= 1000
    - Shard 2 ->  UserId > 1000 && userId <= 2000
    - Shard 3 -> UserId > 2000 && userId <= 3000

- Each shard will contain the same schema (tables) and
the information will be saved based on the rules. 

- When doing Shard in serverless like DynamoDB, we will
pick a partition key and AWS will be in charge of the
partitions based on the key.

elements.text:
- Re-Sharding might be complex cause adding a new
server (shard) will require to re-distribute the data. How
do i figure out what data gets send to the new host
and get removed from the other host?  

- HotSpots (Celebrity problem), the way we distribute
the data across shards it has to keep in mind the
traffic. If there is one shard containing information that
will be query a lot, then we might need to think about
that when distributing.

elements.text:
A data lake is a centralized storage system used to store large amounts of raw, structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data. Unlike a data warehouse, which stores
cleaned and modeled data for reporting, a data lake keeps data in its original format so it can later be processed for analytics, machine learning, auditing, or business
intelligence. A common example is using Amazon S3 as the storage layer, with tools like Glue, Athena, Spark, or Redshift to catalog, query, and process the data.

Unlike a data warehouse, which stores cleaned and modeled data for reporting, a data lake keeps data in its original format so it can later be processed for analytics, machine learning, auditing, or business intelligence. A common example is using Amazon S3 as the storage layer, with tools like Glue, Athena, Spark, or Redshift to catalog, query, and process the data.

elements.text:
Raw data is stored in S3, commonly as JSON, CSV, logs, or other source formats.

AWS Glue can run ETL jobs to extract raw data from S3, transform it by cleaning,
validating, deduplicating, enriching, or converting it, and then load the curated
result back into S3.

The curated data is often stored in optimized formats like Parquet and
partitioned by common query filters such as year, month, day, country, region, or
tenant.

AWS Glue Data Catalog stores metadata about the data in S3, such as schemas,
table definitions, file formats, S3 locations, and partitions.

Athena is a serverless SQL query engine that queries data directly from S3 using
metadata from the Glue Data Catalog.

Redshift is a data warehouse for analytics and BI workloads. It can either load
curated data from S3 into Redshift tables or query S3 directly using Redshift
Spectrum.

elements.text:
A fleet of other servers that are sitting along
side the application servers.

Main Goal, is to reduce load on the database and
improve response times

Job - Keep in memory copies of data that's been
going to that database. So it can keep track of
the most hits or popular ones in the database.

- We can also scale that caching fleet
independently. 

- It can be beneficial to have this layer
separated from the web servers so that they can
scale independently.
